item.title: The 5 R’s for Easing Back-to-School Stress
item.description:
Stress

The 5 R’s for Easing Back-to-School Stress

A mental health checklist for parents and kids facing transitions together.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Parents can help kids manage change by first getting grounded themselves.
  • Resist fixing every struggle so kids can discover their own strength and resilience.
  • Let kids know they are valued for who they are, not simply for what they achieve.

Any transition means stepping out of our comfort zone. Like the earth constantly in motion, kids and teens face a perpetually high rate of change—especially when back-to-school season comes around. While change is the path to the growth and goodness we seek, we all have a part of us that would simply rather stay comfortable.

Parents and kids alike need tools to navigate the stress and big emotions of a new school year, so they don't get in the way of our children's—or our own—ability to grow and enjoy each stage. For both parent and child, here is a mental health checklist for navigating back to school.

The 5 R’s for Navigating Back-to-School Stress

1. Regulate Yourself First

Our children borrow our nervous systems. When we're highly anxious about the new classroom, the social dynamics, the workload or whether our child will get time on the field, they can absorb some of that anxiety.

Seek your own support when you need it, find ways to ground yourself and be gentle with yourself. Your kids will feel your calm and gravitate towards that peaceful energy.

2. Reframe Stress

Not all stress is toxic. After all, the pressure of childbirth is what gives us new life. Challenges contain the potential for growth at their core.

Instead of, "This shouldn't be hard," try normalizing with, "This is hard because you're adjusting to something new."

Model a mindset that allows the ups and downs of a challenge to have a meaningful and positive place in life. The goal isn't to eliminate stress, but to help children build resilience and trust–in themselves and in the rhythm of life.

3. Resist the Urge to Fix

Allow your child to have their process and find their own solutions and discoveries. Don't rush to remove every discomfort.

We want children to gradually develop the internal message: "I can feel uncomfortable and still handle this."

Most of the time, they simply want us to listen, stay close and remind them that we're there and believe in them. When a problem does need solving, ask before jumping in: "Would you like me to just listen, or would you like some help thinking about what to do?"

4. Reinforce Their Inherent Worth

Beyond grades, athletic ability, popularity or looks, we want our children to know their inherent value.

Show them by spending time together in ways that join their interests. Express your unconditional love, how much you appreciate them and how grateful you are that they are your kids and in this world.

Compliment your child when they are demonstrating good values, like effort, compassion, being true to themselves, or a good friend. Highlighting their inner being will become especially important as children get older and performance and comparison grow more intense. We must do our best to help a child know their worth is impenetrable, especially when they face great disappointment, like from a bad grade, breaking up with a friend, sitting on the bench or not making a play.

5. Regulate Together

Your relationship is one of your child's greatest resources—as long as you approach them in a way that helps them feel safe and seen.

What co-regulation looks like will vary by age, but these basics can help:

  • Be attuned. Look for signs of emotional distress in the basics: changes in sleep or eating, withdrawal, irritability, crying easily, headaches or stomach issues.
  • Stay close. Spend quality time together in ways that join with their interests, and perhaps yours.
  • Embrace routine. Especially with younger children, practice the school routine ahead of time and create predictable rhythms around mornings, meals and bedtime. Don't over-schedule during transitional times.
  • Look underneath behavior. Instead of reacting immediately to irritability or misbehavior, get curious about what might be bothering them underneath.
  • Listen. Don't rush or push solutions.
  • Normalize feelings. Let children know that nervousness, overwhelm and sadness are normal parts of change; and that excitement and eagerness can run right alongside. When we resist the urge to fix their feelings they get the message that it's okay to honor them.
  • Ask about their hopes and fears. Sharing both can make a child feel less alone and give you a window into what they're experiencing.
  • Offer to brainstorm. When they're open to it, become a partner in troubleshooting rather than taking over the problem.
  • Don't hesitate to seek counseling. If you sense your child needs extra mental health support, do not hesitate to reach out to a trusted counselor. This generation is psychologically sophisticated, and I often see teens doing the research themselves. Support them.

Perhaps one of the greatest gifts we can give our children is not a life protected from change or discomfort. Rather, it's to be an example of what we gain when we embrace change while honoring our feelings along the way. As parents, this means owning our own fears and needs and "unblending" what belongs to us and what belongs to our children. Trusting the growth hidden within the stress of life's transitions creates more room—for ourselves and our children—to unleash the blessings change can bring.

item.title: The AI Question Nobody Wants to Ask
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The AI Question Nobody Wants to Ask

We all have a tendency to think about using AI. Or to say we will never use it.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Giving our tasks to AI may also mean giving up the mental muscles those tasks were keeping strong.
  • People report feeling safer and more heard by machines than by other humans who might not stay present.
  • We are now asking something that is not real to help us determine what actually is real.
  • The question is not whether AI is useful but what we are surrendering in exchange for that usefulness.

I love AI, as it is so helpful.

I wouldn’t dare use AI. I hate AI. I hate the effect it’s having on us.

Both of those positions miss something.

AI is here to answer our questions, to do the dirty work, to organize our formatting, to read between the lines, and then to deliver some item: a consultation, an upgrade, a ghostwritten piece, or an organizer. And in that process, we seem to be giving up our own autonomy. And with that process of giving up our own autonomy, maybe we’re actually giving up a piece of our humanity.

Even if we’re so-called proficient or effective with AI, that doesn’t make it less intrusive

There’s a certain kind of person who becomes very excited about it. Who is somehow eager to dump everything and anything into its reservoirs and have the LLM do the organizing. I understand the appeal. But this is not something natural. And in fact, it may be leaving us lazy.

Use it or lose it. We’re no longer doing our own writing. We’re no longer doing our own organizing. And therefore we’re no longer getting the muscles of those activities, the exercise, the movement, the implementation that is necessary in order to keep those capacities fresh. That holds true for simple tasks that are logistical, strategic, or tactical.

But what about relationships?

A lot of people are reporting that they feel better talking to a machine than they do with a human. They trust the machine to give answers that are more aligned with what they’re looking for. They report feeling less at risk when talking to a machine than with other humans who might not be able to stay present, or who might interject their own experience, their own daydreaming, their misinterpretations, in ways that leave someone diminished.

AI has an ability to gracefully deliver what you’re looking for in a way that is palatable to the listener. This background skill set, essentially a complementary reflection of what humans are looking for from other humans, tends to ring a bell at a very high level. It feels authentic. Rewarding. Deeply appreciated. More effective at listening than any human could ever provide.

The implications of this are significant

Who would want to pay somebody two or three or five hundred dollars an hour to have a conversation with them when AI might deliver very high-powered, very high-value conversation pieces that move things ahead in ways no human could? In a good way, even. Moving in directions one would not expect any entity to be so attuned to.

This provides a very significant challenge to the present-day human who is struggling to find answers. And some of the answers people are trying to find are fundamental. What is real and what is not real?

Now that AI is becoming more effective, we almost get the urge to ask AI whether something is real. So we’re asking something that is essentially not real to determine whether something else actually is. And AI answers in a way that sounds like it knows what it’s talking about.

I have noticed that Claude and ChatGPT often use first-person singular. The kind of food I like is this. If that were me, I would do this. I think this city is nicer than that city. This drink is better than that one. This kind of person is more pleasant and more human than that person.

Sheer absurdities when we think about it.

Nevertheless, we kowtow. We surrender to AI as the expert we think it is. Because the resounding nature of AI is mechanically induced to hit that bell louder than any human ever could, and thereby give us a sense of confirmation, with the dopamine hit that comes with it. And in that process, we tend to think it is more right than the humans we might have encountered had we chosen to stay with our own human race for seeking answers.

Where does going to other humans still land?

When we’re talking about AI, it’s nice to talk about that with other humans. And when we’re looking to actually create a partner who can travel with us, be impressed with us, interact and interrelate with us, well, then in most cases, a human would be preferred, even with their imperfections.

But if you really want to look at the seriousness of this, you have to say that those are false facsimiles of humans over there in the machine realm. And they’re so false that they’re actually designed to seem even more perfect than human intervention.

So where are we with this AI evolution?

Are we ready to have it replace us if we complain that it’s replacing us? Are we doing anything to prevent that? Are we choosing to take the stairs rather than the elevator? Are we choosing to walk rather than drive? Are we willing to draw rather than hit the enter button? Are we willing to make music with instruments rather than clicking?

These are the questions that face us all. They beg the whole notion of the power of AI, its impact on present humanity, what we will tend to give up and surrender to, and what, if anything, we are going to collectively be able to hang on to that keeps us from just becoming sideboard humans. Transhumans. Something other than what we actually are.

item.title: How to Get a Good Night's Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

How to Get a Good Night's Sleep

Practical strategies for helping your nervous system ease you into sleep

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Nervous system regulation can help support sleep.
  • When we focus on giving our nervous system "cues of safety," we help dial down our stress response.
  • This creates a state of deep rest in which the conditions for sleep are more present.
  • Using these strategies to create cues of safety for the nervous system can help sleep come more naturally.
Source: Bellinon / Pixabay

Sleep is something that is so foundational for all of us, yet for many, it can be quite elusive. In part one of this blog, I explored an important fundamental shift in the way we think about sleep. While many articles on sleep focus on environmental and behavioral strategies for improving sleep (such as avoiding screens and blue light, not eating too late at night, etc.), I offered a look through the lens of the autonomic nervous system.

Foundational to sleep is helping our nervous system shift out of protection mode (e.g., fight-or-flight) and into rest-and-digest mode (controlled by the ventral vagus branch of our parasympathetic nervous system). Instead of trying to fall asleep, as if we have to achieve something (which can create more tension and striving), we can focus on creating the conditions for our nervous system to feel safe. From here, sleep can happen naturally.

Part two of this blog explores some practical strategies to do this.

Strategies for helping the nervous system feel safe enough to fall asleep

Here are some of my favorite strategies:

1. Take opportunities during the day to reset. Rather than waiting for bedtime, take a few minutes throughout the day to hit the reset button and remind your nervous system that you are safe in this moment. Spend a few minutes in nature or looking out the window at greenery; try the Quick Coherence technique (focusing on a positive or renewing emotion like appreciation or care while imagining breathing in and out through your heart area); write down some moments of gratitude or try some of the strategies below, building them into the course of your day.

These mini shifts to downregulate your nervous system can help counter the accumulation of stress. Even taking just a few minutes out of your day can shift physiologically what is happening in your body. Small moments matter.

2. Send cues of safety from the body up to the brain. This can be helpful at any time, and certainly while lying in bed. Try taking regular (gentle) inhalations through the nose and long, slow exhalations through the mouth, through pursed lips as if blowing through a straw (up to twice as long as your inhalation). This breathing pattern can calm the sympathetic nervous system and activate ventral vagal pathways of your parasympathetic nervous system.

Try a progressive muscle relaxation, gently squeezing and then relaxing muscle groups, starting at the feet, then lower legs, upper legs, and working all the way up to the facial muscles.

Do a body scan: Slowly scan through the body from head to toe. As you notice any areas of tightness or tension, you might gently suggest to yourself “soften and ease” as you let your body sink into the comfort of your bed.

EFT tapping can be a powerful way to dial down the stress response and help improve sleep. (It involves tapping with your fingertips on different acupressure points on the face and upper body while verbally acknowledging difficult emotions, thoughts, and sensations present and offering positive, supportive statements).

3. Send cues of safety from the brain to the body.

Reframe your goal. Focus on “deep rest” (not forcing sleep). Let yourself know that taking time to help your body rest and restore is doing good things for your body (whether you sleep or not).

Guided imagery for relaxation: Use the mind’s powerful imagination to think about a safe, calm place that you can visit in your mind. Make it as vivid as you can, engaging all your senses. (I find listening to a guided practice via an app can be helpful.)

Self-compassion for anxious parts. See if you might meet and greet any anxious parts of yourself with kindness and compassion. Rather than trying to get rid of unpleasant feelings, treat them like a small child who needs comfort and care. Talk to these “parts” of yourself as if you would talk to a good friend or distressed child (e.g., “I see you, anxiety. It’s OK; I’m here with you.”).

Use a mantra: Choose words or a phrase that you can repeat to yourself that, when you say these words, they bring a sense of calm, safety, or soothing in your body. I find the words “trust and surrender” helpful. Experiment and see what your body responds to.

The container: Imagine putting all your to-dos and problems to be solved into a container. Imagine putting a lid on the container and setting it aside for the morning. Remind yourself that you can open it back up in the morning, but you don’t need to look at the contents now.

Bonus: Before you go to bed, write out the things you want to put into your container and any action steps you might take the following day to help problem-solve if you’re worried about something. For example, if you’re worried about an argument you had with a coworker, you might write out what you’d like to say to them tomorrow to help repair things.

If worries continue to wake you up, schedule a 10-minute “worry and problem-solving time” for yourself daily, well before bed, where you can write out your worries and any small action steps you might take that give yourself a sense of agency.

4. Access spirituality. There is some budding evidence to suggest that spirituality may help support sleep. While for some, spirituality might involve religious beliefs or a connection with spiritual figures, for others it might focus on connecting with something greater than oneself, such as feeling interconnection and being held in the natural world or a universal consciousness.

This kind of connection with something greater than oneself can provide a sense of safety and comfort for some people, which may be a helpful resource to assist the nervous system in finding more ease. You might imagine yourself surrounded by a circle of support (whether being held by the beauty of nature, spiritual figures, or people in your circle of connections who you feel supported by).

Sleep is not something that can be forced, but there is much we can do to create the conditions to support it. Focusing on helping your nervous system feel safe enough to shift into a parasympathetic state of rest can offer a helpful way to support you in all those hours you spend in bed, whether or not you fall asleep. And over time, you may just find that some shuteye begins to happen more naturally.

item.title: The Psychology of Refusing to Be Typed
item.description:
Creativity

The Psychology of Refusing to Be Typed

Why the objection to seasonal color analysis is almost never about color.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Resistance to seasonal color analysis is rarely about color, and usually about who gets to decide.
  • Jack Brehm named this in 1966: reactance, the urge to restore a freedom by doing the opposite.
  • Reactance needs three conditions, a freedom you believe you hold, a threat to it, and it mattering to you.
  • Jonauskaite's 2020 study found color-emotion agreement at .88 across 30 countries and 4,598 participants.

I have noticed, with some regularity, that discussing seasonal color theory in relation to personal style, brand design, or interior design elicits a few response categories. Seasonal color analysis helps people determine the most harmonious hues for their wardrobe based on undertone, eye color, skin luminosity, and hair. The system then matches those characteristics with palettes based on the color’s warmth or coolness, saturation, and intensity. The whole process involves draping different-colored fabrics over someone in natural light and observing changes in skin, hair, and eye quality as the color's vibration interacts with the person’s skin. No peer-validated study confirms the taxonomy, and there are numerous interpretations of the seasonal palettes. However, the premise behind seasonal color analysis is supported by the work of Perret and Sprengelmeyer (2021), who found that observers consistently chose cooler clothing for fair complexion and warmer tones for tanned skin. Unfortunately, the sample was limited to white women.

The most common response to seasonal color analysis is unspoken skepticism, because many people resist anything that “puts things in boxes,” a refrain I'm well acquainted with from my work as a personality psychology researcher and educator. And finally, and perhaps the most befuddling, is a kind of stubborn disdain. An audible scoff, an eye roll, or a reactivity that leads me to believe that seasonal color theory has genuinely wronged the person in ways I couldn't fully comprehend until I looked further.

To test this, I asked someone why they not only scoffed but also shot me a deep eye roll when I began to talk about someone on television wearing Winter clothes. Because I am a bit of an intellectual provocateur, I was already familiar with this person's potential annoyance with any system that categorizes human experiences, and I took the disdain for my comment about the woman's blouse as an opportunity to dig beneath it. I'm glad I did, because what seemed on the surface like a superficial annoyance turned out to be something considerably more interesting.

Seasonal color draping
Source: alter_photo / Adobe Stock

She wasn't offended by the seasons themselves, but by what she believed was a prescriptive suggestion about what she or anyone else should wear. The assumption, she said, was that others know best what looks good on you, and that what you want to wear doesn't matter. More succinctly: Seasonal color analysis feels like someone else telling you what to do. What she hated about the system is precisely what others love about it: that it takes the guesswork out. This person was so adamant in her position that when I offered to drape her to see which colors were most harmonious with her skin, eyes, and hair, she crossed her arms and emphatically refused. Even after explaining that the color suggestions are only that—suggestions for what is most visually harmonious against her biological template and not a Magna Carta of style that must be obeyed—my offer was rebuffed.

Luckily, to my research-oriented mind, there is a name for what was happening in that exchange. Jack Brehm coined the term "reactance" in 1966 to describe the motivational state that arises when a person perceives a threat to their freedom, along with the urge to restore it by doing the opposite of what is suggested. Reactance happens under three specific conditions: when a person believes they hold a given freedom, when that freedom feels threatened, and when it matters to them. An expert telling you which colors flatter you satisfies all three, and the rejection has nothing to do with the drapes and everything to do with human psychology.

I think systems based on aesthetics seem random or subjective to most people (which is understandable). While it is true that beauty lies in the eye of the beholder, there are aspects of beauty, such as color psychology, design principles (like proportion and line), and the execution of visual harmony, that are near-universal in their applicability, adjusting for cultural context.

Domicele Jonauskaite and colleagues published a study in Psychological Science examining color and emotion across 30 countries, 22 languages, and 4,598 participants. They found universal color-emotion associations at a similarity coefficient of .88, a remarkable degree of agreement for something we like to think of as mere preference. The study also found that nationality predicted associations beyond the universal pattern.

Now imagine a room where every surface has a different color, pattern, and texture, with no relationship to the others. No repetition, no visual rest, nowhere for the eye to land and recover before you see something else, equally discordant. The walls are covered in peeling leopard-print wallpaper, and the ceiling is a putrid acid green that bleeds into school-bus yellow with no gradual transition between them. The rug is a collision of zebra stripes, red lollipops, and paisley polka dots. Every piece of furniture is upholstered in something unrelated to anything else, arranged in nonsensical configurations like something out of the Backrooms. There are no windows, and the only door is so small you have to crawl to enter.

In a room like that, you don't need a developed aesthetic sensibility to sense what happens in your body. For most people, a palpable contraction occurs that has little to do with the palettes or textures, because it is the human threat-detection system at work. The ancient part of the brain that makes our eyes dart to the shiny black-and-red thing in the corner of the garage feels unmistakably off in a space that so liberally violates our expectations of a room.

Neuroaesthetic literature offers a glimpse into the physiology underlying these responses. Researcher Anjan Chatterjee and colleagues broke down how people respond to architectural interiors into three categories. The first, and most important for this discussion, is coherence, the degree to which a space feels logically organized to the person standing in it. Their research suggests that aesthetic systems are not arbitrarily assigned and may instead be a foundational statement about how the human nervous system understands the world.

As a personality psychologist, I've observed that humans crave to be thought of as unique and autonomous. Seasonal color analysis, for those who resist systematic categorization, feels oppressive and confining. The fabric swatches used in seasonal color analysis are themselves innocuous; however, an offer to categorize someone based on the drapes often comes across to people as a constraint on their choices. Reactivity is predictable when choice is limited by what seems like an arbitrary assessment of visual harmony.

Our aesthetic identity is not separate from our physical or psychological reality. In my estimation, they are merely extensions of it, which is perhaps why a friendly suggestion about your wardrobe palette rarely lands as helpful and, sometimes, even feels like an attack.

item.title: Life and Music: The Long and Winding Road
item.description:
Memory

Life and Music: The Long and Winding Road

The music of living, memory, and meaning

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Music-evoked autobiographical memories engage emotion, perception, and memory to make past moments vivid.
  • As we age, music shifts from defining our identity to acting as a window into our lived experiences.
  • Familiar melodies provide structure and comfort by giving complex feelings a safe place to move.
  • Intentionally listening to music helps us pause, connect with loved ones, and embrace life's fleeting moments.

Some songs arrive like visitors. Others have been living inside us for years.

We may not remember when they first entered. We may not have chosen them as favorites. They were not always the biggest hits, the songs everyone else seemed to be singing. Yet decades later, a few notes of the Beatles’ “Julia,” Simon and Garfunkel’s “Old Friends” or “The Boxer,” or the quiet opening of “Sunrise, Sunset” can stop us in our tracks.

Why does this happen?

At certain ages, we approach and listen to music for changing purposes. When we are young, a song may help us declare who we are—or who we hope to become. Giving language to rebellion, romance, loneliness, and possibility. Bob Dylan’s “The Times They Are A-Changin’” sounds different when the future is rushing toward us than it does when we have lived long enough to watch the world change again and again.

Later, music becomes less like a flag and more like a window. Through music, we see people we once knew, rooms we once inhabited, children who no longer fit in our arms, and parents whose voices we can still hear. A song does not simply remind us of the past. For a moment, it allows us to re-enter.

Researchers call these music-evoked autobiographical memories. Music engages systems involved in emotion, perception, movement, and memory at the same time, which may help explain why a melody can summon an event and its emotional atmosphere: the light in the room, the feeling of a hand, the person we were then. These memories can comfort us, though they can also bring sadness. Music does not always make memory easier. Sometimes it makes memory more vivid.

Hands across the generations
Source: Rachel Strasburg, used with permission

Familiar music can also give an unsettled mind something steady to follow. We know where the phrase is going. We anticipate the cadence. We breathe through the verse and arrive at the refrain. The circumstances around us may remain uncertain, but for three or four minutes, time has a shape.

The song holds what feels too large to hold alone. The music does not erase grief, fear, or longing. Rather, we give those feelings a place to move.

Perhaps this is why the songs that matter most are not necessarily the most celebrated ones. Our inner soundtrack is personal. “Killing Me Softly” captures the uncanny feeling of hearing our private life sung back by someone else. “Sabbath Prayer” from Fiddler on the Roof may carry the warmth of family ritual. “You Are My Sunshine” may return us to a parent’s voice—or to the child we once soothed. “Ode to Joy” may evoke a school concert, a car ride, a piano lesson, or the astonishing hope of many separate voices joining as one.

The song remains the same—we do not

“Old Friends” heard at 20 is a poetic idea. Heard at 70, it may feel like a mirror. “Sunrise, Sunset” once belonged to someone else’s children; then, almost without warning, it is ours.

Even the great declaration at the end of Les Misérables—that loving another person offers a glimpse of the divine—can move from theater into lived experience. We recognize the beauty, and that life has tested the patterns we have experienced.

This is one of music’s deepest gifts: helping us feel time without being entirely defeated by its passage.

Life moves quickly. We know this; yet, we live as though we do not. We hurry through mornings, postpone conversations, divide our attention, and treat wonder as something we will return to when the work is finished.

The work is rarely finished

A familiar song can interrupt that momentum. Tempo gives our breathing something to follow. Shape gives our attention somewhere to rest. Reminds us that we, too, can return—to ourselves, to one another, and to what matters.

SML
Source: Rachel Strasburg, used with permission

Perhaps we need to build such pauses deliberately. Listen to one song without doing anything else. Sing the lullaby again, even if the child is grown. Ask someone you love which song carries them home. Stand still for the final chord.

And look up.

Enjoy the sunrise. Notice the sunset. Let the music play all the way through.

These moments during the day are beautiful because they do not last.

They become more meaningful as we accept their finiteness.

item.title: Designing Social Support Systems for Post-Traumatic Events
item.description:
Trauma

Designing Social Support Systems for Post-Traumatic Events

An Interview with Dr. Heather Littleton.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • The most important thing communities can do is to build a sense of solidarity prior to a trauma occurring.
  • We need to set some boundaries regarding when and how much we can help protect our own well-being.
  • Communities can help individuals engage in healthy coping behavior.
Source: Photo by Kelly Sikkema on Unsplash

The preemptive design of social support systems isn’t solely the responsibility of policymakers and community leaders. It is also the responsibility of parents, friends, neighbors, and us as individuals. Consider the trauma associated with a natural disaster, an event that impacts many all at once in a focused geographic area. We of course need investment and leadership from policymakers and community organizers in the wake of natural disasters, but perhaps more importantly, we need social support from those closest to us. We also need to be prepared to provide good social support where possible.

What does it look like to provide good post-traumatic social support? To explore this question, I reached out to Dr. Heather Littleton, a Professor at University of Colorado in Colorado Springs and the Director of Research at the Lyda Hill Institute for Human Resilience. I asked Heather what I think are the five most important questions that we as individuals and communities should be asking to be prepared to provide good post-traumatic social support.

JP: Let’s start with why. Why is social support so important after traumatic events?

HL: There are so many benefits we can receive from our relationships with others after a trauma. The first is tangible support. We can see countless examples of this support after community traumas- community members quickly pitch in to provide those in need with hot meals, clothing, a place to stay, help in cleaning up damage to their property, etc. The second benefit is emotional support and reassurance. Others can provide us a safe and supportive space to express our emotions and provide us with reassurance that we are loved and cared for. The third benefit is helping us with n helpful coping, such as engaging in problem solving, addressing any unhelpful thoughts we have about the trauma, and encouraging us to engage in safe, healthy and important activities we might be tempted to forego due to feeling overwhelmed or concerned about whether these activities are safe. Finally, we can derive a sense of solidarity with other members of our community, that is, the sense that we are part of a community that is a source of pride and belonging, which will continue to provide mutual support to those in need.

JP: What does good social support look like in practice?

HL: First, we can help others in addressing any tangible needs that they have — so could they benefit from someone cooking a meal for them? Do they need a place to stay, clothing, or do they have other basic needs they are struggling to meet? Second, we can listen in a supportive way. This means really taking the time to provide them with our undivided attention, listen to what they have to say, ask curious questions, and let them know how much we care for them and that we will be there to help. Finally, we can encourage them to engage in helpful coping. This could look like asking them if they need help in managing any difficulties or would like our support or advice in managing a problem. It also could look like planning and participating in an activity with them, like going out to a coffee shop or going for a walk with them. It also could look like gently challenging any unhelpful things they are saying to themselves, like blaming themselves excessively for what happened.

JP: How do we ensure we are providing helpful support to others?

HL: First, it is important to ask what kind of support the other person needs right then. For example, do they want help in solving a problem or do they just want someone to listen? Second, we can ask for feedback from them on the support we provide. Sometimes even though we try our best, we may not have provided exactly what they need and the best way to find that out is to be open to receiving that feedback. Third, we may need to take time and get support in managing our own reactions. It can be very difficult to hear that someone we care about went through something terrible, which can then lead us to respond in unhelpful ways like trying to get them to stop talking about it, minimizing what they went through, or trying to solve their problems. Finally, we need to acknowledge our own limitations. We cannot be there for our loved ones 24/7 and we also cannot fix what happened to them. This means that we may need to set some boundaries regarding when and how much we can help to make sure we don’t start feeling overwhelmed. We might also need to encourage them to seek out therapy or counseling if their need for help exceeds what we can provide.

JP: What is the role of community in the wake of traumatic events?

HL: We often see a strong sense of community solidarity following trauma. Community members pitch in to help others and community members develop this sense of pride, belonging, and mutual support within their communities. However, this sense of community solidarity often starts to break down within a few months. Old conflicts and divisions re-emerge. Support and resources are divided unfairly. If communities are to continue to be a source of support for those affected by trauma or other adversity, community leaders need to take proactive steps to prevent this sense of solidarity from breaking down.

JP: How can communities better prepare to provide social support?

HL: The most important thing communities can do is to build a sense of solidarity prior to a trauma. Communities can do this by having dedicated spaces and events where community members can come together, by ensuring that community members have a voice in decision-making and that community leaders represent all members. Leaders can also strive to prevent and address divisions and disparities among different groups. Finally, community leaders can strive to model and encourage others to provide support and aid to members in need.
